Use this page to route a real-data qualifying-exam problem. Define the scientific target before choosing software: the same outcome can require different models when the target is population-average, subject-specific, history-conditional, causal, or predictive.

::: {.callout-important title="Core decision order"}
1. **Outcome type and scale.**
2. **Objective:** description, inference, causal effect, or prediction.
3. **Independent unit and data structure.**
4. **Estimand and model class.**
5. **Missingness or censoring.**
6. **Mean and time structure.**
7. **Covariance, random effects, or working correlation.**
8. **Estimation and model comparison.**
9. **Inference and contrasts.**
10. **Diagnostics, sensitivity, and reporting.**
:::

**Source basis.** The ordering and technical rules synthesize this manual with BIOS767 lecture slides, especially `BIOS-767-Part-009.pdf`, slides 7–8; the 2019, 2020, 2021, 2023, 2024, and 2025 applied exams and worked solutions; and the external [Qual Application Exam Playbook](https://qual-exam-template-book.xinyichen12138.chatgpt.site/template-book). The playbook informed the fast lookup design, not the statistical content.

## 60-second route {#roadmap-60-second-route}

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A["1. Outcome scale"] --> B["2-4. Objective + independent unit<br/>+ estimand/model class"]
  B --> C["5-7. Missingness/censoring<br/>+ mean/time + dependence"]
  C --> D["8-10. Estimate/compare → infer/contrast<br/>→ diagnose/sensitivity/report"]
```

Before modeling, verify coding, denominators, visit ordering, the number of independent units, observations per unit, and whether repeated rows are measurements of one outcome or distinct outcomes. [R workflow: EDA and data structure](../analysis-in-r/01-eda-descriptive.qmd) · [Mathematics: longitudinal foundations](../math-writeups/01-foundations-mvn-ml-reml.qmd)

## Outcome-first lookup {#roadmap-outcome-first}

The table chooses the response distribution and link. If observations are dependent, use the next section to choose a marginal, mixed, transition, or joint formulation.

| Outcome | First model to consider | Escalate or redirect when | Start here |
|---|---|---|---|
| Approximately Gaussian continuous | Gaussian linear model; for repeated data, a Gaussian marginal model or LMM | Heteroscedasticity, nonlinear time, irregular timing, or complex covariance | [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/03-linear-mixed-models.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/03-gaussian-marginal-models.qmd) |
| Positive or right-skewed continuous | Scientifically justified transformation, lognormal model, or **Gamma model with log link** | Skew persists, variance grows with the mean, or zeros require a separate mechanism | [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/05-glm-review.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/06-generalized-linear-models.qmd) |
| Binary or binomial | Logistic or probit GLM; GEE or GLMM for dependence | Separation, sparse cells, repeated outcomes, or clustering | [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/05-glm-review.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/06-generalized-linear-models.qmd) |
| Nominal categorical | Generalized-logit multinomial model | Rows repeat within a unit: use marginal or random-effect dependence | [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/05-glm-review.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/09-ordinal-nominal-joint-models.qmd) |
| Ordinal | Cumulative-logit proportional-odds model | Use partial proportional odds for selected violations; use ordinal GEE or an ordinal mixed model for dependence | [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/05-glm-review.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/09-ordinal-nominal-joint-models.qmd) |
| Count or rate | Poisson log-linear model; include $\log(\text{exposure})$ as an offset for rates | Diagnose extra-Poisson variation; consider negative binomial, zero-inflated, or hurdle models for overdispersion or excess zeros | [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/06-glmm.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/08-generalized-linear-mixed-multilevel.qmd) |
| Multiple distinct outcomes | MANOVA for a continuous response vector, or outcome-specific models joined by shared random effects | Outcomes have different scales or links, repeated timing, or scientific interest in cross-outcome dependence | [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/08-multivariate-testing-pca.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/09-ordinal-nominal-joint-models.qmd) |
| Censored or below a limit of detection | Censored likelihood, Tobit-type model, or censored longitudinal mixed model | Detection limits vary, censoring is informative, or the latent distribution is doubtful | [R workflow for sensitivity concepts](../analysis-in-r/07-missing-data.qmd) · [Mathematics for likelihood concepts](../math-writeups/10-missing-data.qmd) |
| Time to event | Survival model matched to censoring, competing risks, and recurrent-event structure | **Outside this manual:** do not force survival data into a longitudinal GLM | Outside-manual branch |
| Prediction or high-dimensional analysis | Prespecified training, tuning, validation, and calibration workflow | Clustered/repeated rows require resampling by the independent unit; clinical use requires external validation | [R workflow for PCA](../analysis-in-r/08-multivariate-testing-pca.qmd) · [External playbook off-ramp](https://qual-exam-template-book.xinyichen12138.chatgpt.site/template-book) |

::: {.callout-warning title="Do not collapse by reflex"}
Collapsing an ordinal response to binary discards information and changes the response likelihood and estimand. AIC or BIC from the collapsed binary outcome is not directly comparable with AIC or BIC from the original ordinal outcome.
:::

## Objective and independent unit {#roadmap-objective-unit}

| Objective | What the answer must target |
|---|---|
| Description | Observed distributions, trajectories, missingness, and dependence; avoid causal language |
| Inference | A prespecified estimand, model, contrast, uncertainty procedure, and independent sampling unit |
| Causal effect | A treatment/exposure strategy, target population, time zero, confounding assumptions, and design-compatible analysis; randomization supports causal contrasts, whereas observational adjustment requires explicit assumptions |
| Prediction | A future target population and prediction time, leakage-free resampling, calibration, discrimination or error, and external/temporal validation |

The **independent unit** determines clustering, resampling, influence deletion, degrees of freedom, and effective sample size. It may be a person, dyad, physician, clinic, trial, or randomized cluster—not an individual row. Distinguish repeated visits within a subject, members within a dyad, subjects within a site, and crossed or nested levels before writing the model.

## Dependence and estimand {#roadmap-dependence-estimand}

| Scientific target or dependence | Model class and coefficient meaning | Paired references |
|---|---|---|
| Population-average effect | Marginal model or GEE; coefficients describe the population mean | [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/04-marginal-models-gee.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/07-marginal-models-gee.qmd) |
| Subject-specific trajectory, heterogeneity, BLUP, or cluster-specific effect | LMM or GLMM; coefficients condition on random effects and random effects describe heterogeneity | [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/03-linear-mixed-models.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/04-linear-mixed-models.qmd) |
| Effect conditional on response history | Transition model using lagged outcomes or response history; interpret conditionally on that history | [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/06-glmm.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/11-transition-models.qmd) |
| Dependence among distinct outcomes | MANOVA for a continuous vector or a joint-response/shared-random-effect model | [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/08-multivariate-testing-pca.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/09-ordinal-nominal-joint-models.qmd) |
| Marginal mean with covariance modeled directly | Gaussian marginal model; useful when population profiles and a structured covariance are primary | [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/03-linear-mixed-models.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/03-gaussian-marginal-models.qmd) |

Repeated measurements of **one** outcome are not automatically a joint-response problem. Use a joint-response model when there are two or more distinct outcome processes whose cross-outcome dependence matters.

With a Gaussian identity link, the LMM fixed effects describe both the marginal mean $E(Y_i\mid X_i)=X_i\beta$ and the conditional mean at $b_i=0$. With nonlinear links, integrating over random effects changes the mean: GEE and GLMM coefficients generally target different estimands and have different magnitudes. Do not describe one as a mere robustness version of the other. [Interpretation reference](A2-interpretation-cheatsheet.qmd)

## Missingness and censoring {#roadmap-missingness-censoring}

Classify the problem before choosing a method:

1. **What is absent?** Outcome, covariate, visit, entire unit, or a structurally undefined outcome.
2. **What is the pattern?** Monotone dropout or intermittent missingness.
3. **What assumption is proposed?** MCAR, MAR, or MNAR, stated conditionally on recorded history and covariates.
4. **Is it actually censoring?** A detection limit or censoring event supplies partial information about the value; it is not ordinary missingness.

Missingness mechanisms generally cannot be proven from observed data. State the assumption, explain why it may be plausible, and stress-test departures.

| Situation or method | Working rule |
|---|---|
| Ordinary complete-case or available-case GEE | Generally requires conditional MCAR; ordinary available-case GEE is not generally valid under MAR |
| IPW-GEE | Can address MAR if the observation-probability model is correct and positivity holds; account for estimated weights |
| Compatible multiple imputation | Can address MAR for missing outcomes or covariates when the imputation model preserves the analysis model, timing, and dependence |
| Gaussian likelihood or GLMM likelihood | Uses all observed outcomes under ignorable MAR when the outcome model is correct and parameters are distinct |
| MNAR | Requires identifying assumptions and sensitivity analysis, such as selection models, pattern-mixture models, or delta adjustments |
| Missing covariates | Not automatically solved by an outcome likelihood; use a joint model, compatible MI, weighting, or a justified complete-case argument |
| Limit of detection or censoring | Use the inequality/event information in a censored likelihood or justified sensitivity method; do not recode as ordinary missing |
| Structural absence or truncation by death | Redefine the estimand and target population; a post-death outcome is undefined, not merely unobserved |

For MI, fit the **same analysis model in every imputed dataset** and pool the same estimable function with Rubin's rules. For IPW or MI, diagnose weights or imputations—not only the final outcome model. [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/07-missing-data.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/10-missing-data.qmd)

## Mean and time specification {#roadmap-mean-time}

| Decision | Practical rule |
|---|---|
| Preliminary mean | Use a saturated profile mean when feasible; otherwise use the largest scientifically reasonable mean. Do not blindly saturate when visits are numerous, timing is irregular, or sample size is inadequate. |
| Time representation | Categorical visit permits arbitrary profiles; continuous time is parsimonious. Consider centered linear, polynomial, or spline trajectories. Center time so main effects answer a meaningful question. |
| Effect modification over time | Include treatment-by-time or group-by-time interactions when trajectory differences are the target. Report derived means, slopes, or contrasts at meaningful times. |
| Baseline | In randomized studies, use design-compatible baseline adjustment or a justified constrained longitudinal model; in observational studies, do not force baseline group equality. |
| Confounding | Retain prespecified confounders regardless of their individual p-values. Selection by p-value does not establish confounding control. |
| Time-varying covariates | Distinguish systematic from stochastic covariates; separate within- and between-unit components when relevant; consider histories and lags. Endogenous covariates and time-varying confounding affected by prior treatment require more than ordinary regression. |

[R workflow: EDA and profiles](../analysis-in-r/01-eda-descriptive.qmd) · [Mathematics: Gaussian means](../math-writeups/03-gaussian-marginal-models.qmd) · [Mathematics: time-varying covariates](../math-writeups/12-time-varying-covariates.qmd)

## Model selection and estimation {#roadmap-selection-estimation}

### Canonical Gaussian procedure {#roadmap-gaussian-procedure}

1. Begin with a rich preliminary mean.
2. Choose a plausible preliminary covariance; use unstructured only when the number and regularity of visits and the sample size support it.
3. Compare mean structures under **ML**, holding the covariance family fixed.
4. With the selected mean held fixed, compare covariance or random-effect structures, preferably under **REML**.
5. Recheck the mean–covariance pairing and iterate if needed.
6. Refit the final Gaussian model under **REML**.
7. Perform cluster-aware diagnostics.

This order follows BIOS767 Part 9, slides 7–8: reduce the mean first, then check whether the preliminary covariance remains suitable. [R workflow](../analysis-in-r/03-linear-mixed-models.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/03-gaussian-marginal-models.qmd)

### Test and criterion rules {#roadmap-test-criteria}

| Task | Estimation/comparison rule |
|---|---|
| Gaussian fixed-effect comparison | Fit candidates by **ML**; use a justified nested LRT or Wald test, or ML AIC/BIC for comparable nonnested likelihoods |
| Gaussian covariance or random-effect comparison | Hold fixed effects identical; **REML is preferred** for covariance estimation/comparison |
| Final Gaussian marginal model or LMM | Refit by **REML** |
| GLM, GLMM, or ordinal likelihood model | Fit by **ML**; check integration accuracy for GLMMs |
| GEE | No ML or REML; use robust Wald/score-type inference and QIC/CIC-type criteria for comparable candidates |
| Quasi-Poisson | No ordinary AIC and no ordinary likelihood-ratio test because there is no full likelihood |
| Transition model | Use the conditional likelihood and compare models on the same transitions and conditioning sample |
| Multiple imputation | Fit the same model and estimable function in every imputation; combine with Rubin pooling rather than pooling data or p-values |

A standard likelihood-ratio test requires:

- nested models;
- the same response observations and likelihood;
- identical fixed-effect designs for REML comparisons; and
- an interior null parameter.

For a variance-zero boundary hypothesis, do not automatically use an ordinary chi-square reference. Use a justified mixture distribution, restricted LRT, or parametric bootstrap. [Inference and diagnostic mathematics](../math-writeups/05-inference-diagnostics.qmd) · [R reference](A1-inference-diagnostics.qmd)

Use **LRT** for nested comparable likelihood models; **Wald, Kenward–Roger, or Satterthwaite** procedures for prespecified fixed-effect contrasts and small-sample LMM inference; **AIC/BIC** for comparable likelihoods fitted to the same response data; **QIC/CIC** for comparable GEE candidates; and **cross-validation or external validation** for prediction. Record model-selection uncertainty when the final inferential model was chosen from the same data.

## Inference and interpretation {#roadmap-inference}

Inference comes after the estimand and model are defined.

| Target | Procedure and interpretation |
|---|---|
| Prespecified effect | Write an estimable function $L\beta$ or joint hypothesis $L\beta=c$; report estimate, uncertainty, scale, and independent unit |
| Interaction | A main effect is evaluated at the reference levels and time origin. Prefer estimated means or slopes at meaningful times over isolated polynomial or spline coefficients |
| Repeated profile | Use parallelism, coincidence, and flatness tests when they answer the scientific question; follow with prespecified profile contrasts |
| Nonlinear link | Interpret on both link and response scales when useful: odds ratios for logits, rate ratios for log links, exposure-adjusted rates with offsets, and cumulative odds for ordinal models |
| Dependence-specific estimand | Label the result population-average, subject-specific/cluster-specific, or conditional on response history |
| Family of contrasts | Define the family and apply a justified multiplicity adjustment |
| Covariance estimate | State whether uncertainty is model-based or robust/sandwich and why |

[R workflow: repeated-measures contrasts](../analysis-in-r/02-rm-anova-manova.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/02-repeated-measures-anova-manova.qmd) · [Interpretation reference](A2-interpretation-cheatsheet.qmd)

## Diagnostics by model class {#roadmap-diagnostics}

| Model class | Minimum diagnostic set |
|---|---|
| Universal | Verify coding, denominators, sample and cluster counts, visit order, convergence, implausible estimates, and influence at the independent-unit level |
| Gaussian marginal model or LMM | Raw and Cholesky-normalized residuals; marginal and conditional residuals; residual-versus-time and residual-versus-fitted plots; Q-Q plots; variograms; Mahalanobis distance; subject-level Cook distances/DFBETAs; covariance identifiability and singular fits |
| GLM | Pearson and deviance residuals; binned residuals for binary means; calibration; leverage/influence; dispersion; separation or sparse cells |
| GEE | Cluster ordering and sizes; fitted working correlation; robust versus model-based SEs; cluster influence; residual mean patterns; few-cluster corrections when asymptotics are weak |
| GLMM | Optimizer convergence, gradients, and singularity; quadrature sensitivity; simulation-based residuals; overdispersion; zero inflation; random-effect identifiability |
| Missing-data analysis | Positivity and weight tails; influence of truncation/stabilization; imputation-chain convergence; observed-versus-imputed plausibility; sensitivity to MAR/MNAR assumptions |
| Prediction | Leakage prevention; resampling by independent unit; tuning inside resampling; discrimination or error; calibration; temporal and external validation |

[R diagnostics](A1-inference-diagnostics.qmd) · [Mathematics](../math-writeups/05-inference-diagnostics.qmd)

## Sensitivity and reporting checklist {#roadmap-sensitivity-reporting}

- [ ] State the objective, independent unit, target population, outcome scale, and estimand.
- [ ] Report the full mean, link, offset, time basis, interaction, and dependence specification.
- [ ] Explain the ML, REML, estimating-equation, imputation, weighting, or prediction procedure.
- [ ] Compare scientifically plausible mean/time, covariance/random-effect, link, working-correlation, or distributional alternatives.
- [ ] Examine whether influential units, few clusters, sparse outcomes, or convergence decisions change conclusions.
- [ ] State the missingness/censoring assumptions; add MAR and MNAR sensitivity analyses when consequential.
- [ ] Report prespecified contrasts with multiplicity control and acknowledge model-selection uncertainty.
- [ ] For prediction, report leakage controls, resampling unit, calibration, discrimination/error, and external validity.
- [ ] Translate estimates to the scientific scale and distinguish association, causal effect, and prediction.

## Applied-exam cross-check {#roadmap-applied-exams}

::: {.callout-tip title="Recurring routes in available exams"}
| Exam | Patterns handled by this roadmap |
|---|---|
| 2019 | Longitudinal binary GLMM/GEE and marginal-versus-conditional interpretation; ordinal proportional-odds models; repeated-measures power |
| 2020 | Clustered nominal physician choices; multilevel binary GLMM across trials; multiple correlated binary outcomes |
| 2021 | Poisson rates and variance alternatives; logistic regression; LMM selection; dropout and power; dyadic outcomes |
| 2023 | IPW and MI; logistic prediction; LMM mean selection and trajectory contrasts |
| 2024 | Censored longitudinal biomarkers; ordinal continuation-ratio models; clustering; held-out and external validation |
| 2025 | Stepped-wedge count GLMM/GEE; LMM versus GEE; ordinal outcomes; measurement-error and high-dimensional warnings |

The local 2022 applied-exam PDF is unavailable, so no 2022 coverage is inferred.
:::
